description: Automatic-sequence theory can also be used negatively: any automatic model that directly encodes prime-side membership is likely too rigid. This card turns classification theorems for multiplicative automatic sequences into a falsifier for overly simplistic conjectures about T.
mathematical_formalization: Define a candidate sign map \chi(p)\in\{\pm1\} by whether prime p first appears on row 1 or column 1, and extend completely multiplicatively. If \chi were k-automatic, classification results force eventual character-like rigidity incompatible with observed composite leader placement; therefore any finite-state model must act on frontier states, not on \chi alone.
analogical_connections: compiler IR too weak for source semantics
implementation_hypothesis: Encode candidate low-state automata for prime-side labels, propagate them to composites, and search for contradictions against observed row/column leaders. Small-state infeasibility certificates prune the conjecture space before positive model building.
experiment_seed: Run a SAT/SMT search over k-automatic sign models with a small state budget using the first few hundred assigned primes and border composites as constraints.

closest_prior_art.title: Automatic proofs in combinatorial game theory

novelty_claim: The new move is to use automatic-sequence rigidity as a conjecture filter for the prime-separator frontier, not as a direct generative model.
differentiation: This card is deliberately a negative result generator: it rules out symbolic models that conflate prime-side multiplicativity with the actual mex frontier state.
